column5: angel sent ahead to guard the way and bring Israel to a prepared place
column6: The commentary's guide goes before the weak traveler and brings the road to its appointed home; God sends an angel before Israel to guard it on the way and bring it to the place prepared.

column5: communal fast to seek from God a straight way
column6: The commentary's plural petition asks God directly for the straight path; Ezra proclaims a communal fast to seek from God a straight way for us, the children, and the journey's goods.

column5: ark goes ahead so Israel knows an untraveled way
column6: The commentary says guidance is following a precursor rather than holding a map; Israel lets the ark go before it so that it may know a route it has never traveled.

column5: compassionate guide leads to springs of water
column6: The commentary connects guidance, water, and protection on the journey; Isaiah's compassionate God leads and guides the people by springs so that hunger, thirst, and scorching sun do not overwhelm them.

column5: lost sheep made to wander by their shepherds
column6: The commentary contrasts the guide who knows the path with one who cannot lead and the flock that becomes lost; Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep whose shepherds caused them to wander and forget their resting place.

column5: way in wilderness and rivers in desert
column6: The commentary's straight road is both a route for a traveler and a life-giving course with water; God promises a new way in wilderness and rivers in the desert.

column5: valleys raised, rough ground leveled, crooked made straight
column6: The commentary expands mustaqīm through uprightness, leveling, and an unequally leaning scale; Isaiah's prepared divine road is made by raising, lowering, straightening, and smoothing its terrain.

column5: crooked paths, no justice, no way of peace
column6: The commentary joins straightness, just balance, and the abode of peace; Isaiah describes the inverse, where those without justice make crooked paths and do not know the way of peace.

column5: righteous walk the Lord's right ways; transgressors stumble
column6: The commentary's path is right not merely by name but because it carries its walkers upright while the lost fall away; Hosea says the Lord's ways are right, the righteous walk in them, and transgressors stumble.

column5: lost sheep asks God to seek the servant
column6: The commentary's flock has a guide while 1:7 names those who lose the road; the psalm ends by admitting, like a lost sheep, the need for God to seek the servant.

column5: examination followed by a plea to lead in the everlasting way
column6: The commentary treats guidance as a prayer renewed even by people already addressing God; this psalm asks God to expose a harmful way in the speaker and then lead him in the enduring way.

column5: a way that seems right but ends in death
column6: The commentary insists that a road's destination distinguishes it from a mere direction; Proverbs warns that a path appearing right to a person can nevertheless end in death.

column5: trust, divine help, and making ways straight
column6: The commentary pairs the request for help with the request for the straight road; Sirach tells the hearer to trust God for help and to make the ways straight in hope.

column5: Wisdom guides a fleeing righteous person on straight paths
column6: The commentary develops guidance as accompanying a literal traveler and bringing one toward God's realm; personified Wisdom guides a righteous fugitive on straight paths and shows him God's kingdom.

column5: a good angel accompanies the journey and returns the traveler safely
column6: The commentary's guide goes with a traveler toward a homeward destination; Tobit's reassurance is that a good angel will accompany Tobiah, make the journey succeed, and bring him back safely.

column5: traveler turns body or heart toward the Holy of Holies
column6: The commentary treats direction and direct prayer as inseparable even for a moving traveler; the Mishnah directs a rider who cannot face the sanctuary bodily to direct the heart toward it.

column5: following the light avoids darkness and gains life's light
column6: The commentary's guide leads a traveler who might otherwise be lost in darkness; Jesus says that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.

column5: walking in light before darkness overtakes and obscures the destination
column6: The commentary's road has markers and can be lost; Jesus warns listeners to walk while they have the light, because the one walking in darkness does not know where he is going.

column5: worshiping God according to the Way
column6: The commentary says worship of God is itself the straight road; Paul describes his worship of Israel's God as taking place according to the Way that opponents call a sect.

column5: God keeps the traveler wherever he goes and brings him home
column6: The commentary's road ends in a place of acceptance and needs help along the way; God promises Jacob presence and protection wherever he goes, followed by return to the promised land.

column5: God provides a way out of testing that can be endured
column6: The commentary puts divine help beside a path where the adversary waits; Paul describes God as making a way out within testing so that believers can endure it.

column5: Abraham obeys a call to go without knowing the destination
column6: The commentary rejects a merely detached map in favor of being led along a road; Abraham goes in obedience to God's call even though he does not know where he is going.

column5: Christ leaves an example so believers follow his steps
column6: The commentary's guide advances before those who follow; Peter makes Christ's suffering an exemplar whose steps believers are called to follow.
